function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run from a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **⚠️ Important** – The helper functions in the “Tools” section are only useful for generating *Python* Dockerfiles/K8s manifests.  
> Since this repo is a Node.js project, I’m writing the files manually instead of calling those functions.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re on a machine that doesn’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
# ---------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and includes the latest LTS Node version.  
> * Installing only production deps keeps the image lean.  
> * The app in this repo listens on port **3000** (adjust if your `index.js` uses a different port).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` (or place the files wherever you prefer) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Tip:**  
> If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port` accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            .

      # Push the image to GHCR
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> 2. Builds a Docker image from the repo’s `Dockerfile`.  
> 3. Tags it with the commit SHA and `latest`.  
> 4. Pushes both tags to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  

> **Prerequisites**  
> * No extra secrets are needed because the workflow uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`.  
> * Make sure the repo owner has permission to push to `ghcr.io`.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the login/action and image names accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

> If you created the `k8s/` directory in a different location, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After the push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and publish the Docker image.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify the Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Run the container to make sure it starts
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
```

If you see the expected output (e.g., “Server listening on port 3000”), everything is wired correctly.

---

That’s it! 🎉  
You now have a fully‑functional Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that builds & publishes the image whenever you push to `main`.
